titel: Setting up a savings plan and sticking with it
kurz: How to choose the amount, frequency and execution date of a savings plan, and why the cost-averaging effect is an advantage for investment behaviour but not for returns.

bloecke.md:
A savings plan is a standing order in which the money flows into a fund instead of into an account. It is defined by four details: amount, frequency, execution date and security. Everything else depends on the investor's behaviour.

In Germany and continental Europe, around 15.1 million savings plan instalments were executed per month in 2025, about 40% more than in the previous year.

The primary purpose of a savings plan is to eliminate a decision that recurs every month. A higher return is not its main purpose. An investor who reconsiders each time whether the moment is favourable makes twelve timing decisions a year. Morningstar measures the consequences of these decisions as the gap between fund returns and investor returns. In the decade to the end of 2025, the funds themselves returned 9.9% a year, whereas the average dollar invested earned only 8.7%. The difference of 1.2 percentage points arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales. It grows with volatility and amounts to 0.4 points in the calmest fifth of funds and 2.1 points in the most volatile.

## Date, amount and frequency

The execution date should be at the beginning of the month, shortly after your salary arrives. This has nothing to do with better prices. Money that is still sitting in the current account is easily spent on other things. A good date is two to three banking days after your salary arrives, because a failed execution is not made up later.

When it comes to the amount, durability matters more than size. The instalment should be set so that it can survive a bad month without the arranged overdraft having to be used. It therefore comes only after the emergency fund and any outstanding consumer debt. An instalment that has to be cancelled after two years was too high; an instalment that is never adjusted is too low.

schritte.text: The savings plan collects the instalment from the settlement account rather than from the current account. There must therefore be a balance in the settlement account, or a direct debit mandate must be in place.
Not every ETF is available as a savings plan with every provider. Promotional lists of fee-free funds can end at any time.

schritte.titel: Set the amount, frequency and date
schritte.text: The normal case is a monthly frequency. Minimum instalments are in some cases as low as €1 at neobrokers and usually €25 or €50 at direct banks.

The exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag) should be in place before the debit; otherwise the bank first deducts tax and only refunds it afterwards (Section 44b(5) EStG). The advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) is booked as early as the first days of January.

schritte.titel: Put an increase date in the calendar
schritte.text: On a fixed date each year, the instalment is adjusted to your income. Without such a date, the adjustment does not happen.

bloecke.md: Of all the settings of a savings plan, the frequency is the most overrated. If you buy weekly instead of monthly at the end of the month, each instalment reaches the market around twelve days earlier on average. At a return of 6% a year, this gives about 0.19% more final value, around €560 over 30 years in the illustrative calculation below. With execution at the beginning of the month, as recommended above, this lead disappears; with weekly purchases, the money is then invested later on average. The difference is measurable but small compared with the execution fee.

At some direct banks, each savings plan execution costs a fixed percentage of the instalment. With a fee of 1.75% and an instalment of €300, that is €5.25 per execution and €63 a year. This is more than a world ETF causes in total ongoing fund costs on a portfolio value of a few thousand euros.

The fee acts like a permanent cut of 1.75% in every instalment. In the illustrative calculation with €300 over 30 years at 6%, it reduces the final value by around €5,300. That is about ten times what switching from monthly to weekly brings in at most.

A “free” savings plan at a neobroker also causes costs. They are contained in the execution price, for example in the spread between the buying and selling price, instead of in a separate fee line. Inducements from the trading venue, which used to be a source of income for these providers, have been banned since 1 July 2026.

## The cost-averaging effect recalculated

Advertising for savings plans almost always relies on the same claim. When prices are low, you automatically buy more units, and when they are high, fewer; the average purchase price is therefore below the average price. The claim is true, but it says nothing about the return.

bloecke.formel: Average purchase price = Sum of all instalments ÷ Sum of all units bought
bloecke.erklaerung: The average purchase price is therefore a harmonic mean of the prices rather than an arithmetic one. Mathematically, a harmonic mean is always below the arithmetic mean as soon as the prices fluctuate at all. The effect therefore occurs with every price path, including one that only falls.
bloecke.beispiel: Six instalments of €300 at prices of 100/80/60/80/100/120 buy 21.0 units. The average purchase price is 1,800 ÷ 21.0 = €85.71, whereas the average of the six prices is €90.00.

bloecke.titel: Three price paths, €1,800 each in six monthly instalments (illustrative calculation)
Result after six months as a percentage of €1,800 (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: In all three cases, the average purchase price is below the average of the prices, but the savings plan beats the lump-sum investment only where prices became cheaper along the way.

bloecke.md:
The table shows where the apparent advantage comes from. The savings plan beats the lump-sum investment exactly when its average purchase price is below the entry price. For this, the price must fall below the entry price at some point along the way. If the market rises steadily, the savings plan, at 22.3%, lags well behind the 50% of the lump-sum investment. If the market falls steadily, the savings plan loses less, namely 29.5% instead of 50%.

The reason for this is simple and has nothing to do with average prices. With a savings plan, only about half of the money is invested on average over the investment period. Less market risk means lower expected returns and a narrower dispersion of outcomes, both upwards and downwards. The cost-averaging effect therefore describes a lower average market exposure and is not a source of additional return.

Investors who save monthly because their salary arrives monthly are not exploiting any special effect. They do not have any more money than that. For them, the savings plan is the only possible form and at the same time the one that best protects against behavioural mistakes.

Investors who already have a sum and deliberately invest it in instalments are making a different decision. They give up expected return in order to reduce the dispersion of the outcome. This can be sensible, but the forgone return is then the price of this protection, not a gain.

## Lump sum and phased entry

In the second case, the numbers favour the lump-sum investment, because stock markets rise more often than they fall. An investor who spreads an existing sum over twelve months keeps it in the market for half a year less on average. In terms of expected value, the investor thereby gives up around half of one year's return. A much-cited Vanguard study from 2012 recalculated this for the US, the UK and Australia over rolling twelve-month windows. The immediate lump-sum investment came out ahead in roughly two out of three cases. The exact proportion depends on the country and period; the direction does not.

In the remaining third, the lump-sum investment came out behind, and experience shows that it is precisely these cases that stick in the memory. Investors who know that they would sell if they had invested immediately before a setback should phase their entry. The phasing should then follow a fixed rule: set the tranches and dates in advance, plan for six to twelve months at most, and do not stop when prices fall. A phased entry that is abandoned misses its purpose.

Two investors each pay in €108,000, and both expect 6% a year (illustrative calculation, before tax and costs).

- Investor A saves €300 a month for 30 years and reaches a final value of around €301,000.
- Investor B saves €900 a month for 10 years and then leaves the portfolio untouched for 20 years. B's final value is around €488,000.

The difference of around €187,000 arises solely because B's money was in the market for considerably longer on average. Behind this is the same relationship as with the lump-sum investment, only on a larger scale.

## Adjusting the monthly contribution

A fixed instalment loses purchasing power and its share of income every year. A saver who starts with €300 in 2026 and never changes the instalment saves considerably less in real terms in 2046 than at the start. A fixed rule for pay rises achieves more than any optimisation of returns. Under this rule, a fixed portion of every pay rise goes into the monthly contribution before the extra money is earmarked for consumption. Some providers offer automatic escalation for this, usually at 1% to 10% a year.

bloecke.titel: Constant instalment and 3% escalation over 30 years at 6% p.a. (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: In the escalating variant, around €171,000 instead of €108,000 is paid in over the term, and the final value is around €420,000 instead of €301,000. The last monthly instalment is then around €707.

bloecke.md: Just over half of the additional amount of around €119,000 consists of extra money paid in, namely €63,000. The rest is compound interest on these contributions. That is the purpose of escalation, because it raises the savings rate without a decision being needed every year.

## The savings plan in a market slump

A slump shows whether a savings plan is fulfilling its purpose. After a fall of 35%, the same instalment buys around 54% more units than before (1 ÷ 0.65 = 1.54). These purchases have the greatest effect in the recovery, and they are lost if the savings plan is paused.

The pattern is well known and measurable. The investor return gap identified by Morningstar is greatest where prices fluctuate most. In the most volatile fifth of funds, it is more than 2 percentage points a year, whereas for broad, calm US large-cap funds it is zero. The return is therefore lost through getting in and out of the market rather than through the product itself.

However, these findings are also disputed. Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan argue in the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026 that poor timing costs investors considerably less than Morningstar reports. The practical advice remains the same. Only the estimate of how much it costs not to follow it changes.

1. Suspending instalments during a price decline is the most common and most expensive mistake, because it eliminates the purchases at the lowest prices.
2. An instalment that is too high and has to be paid out of the emergency fund eventually leads to sales at the wrong moment. It is better to start lower and build in escalation.
3. When switching ETFs because another one has recently performed better, units are sold, flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) is incurred, and the tax deferral ends. Instead of one continuous savings plan, the result is two shorter ones.

For savings plans, the advance lump sum is calculated in twelfths for each instalment. Under Section 18(2) InvStG (Investment Tax Act), it is reduced by one twelfth for each full month before the month of acquisition, separately for each savings plan instalment. With twelve instalments of €300 in 2026 and a base interest rate (Basiszins) of 3.20%, this gives an advance lump sum of around €44; with a lump-sum investment in January, it would be around €81. After the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) and 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax, that is around €8 of tax, debited in January 2027. The advance lump sum is therefore far below the saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag). The calculation is simplified. It uses the purchase amount for each instalment and assumes an increase in value at least equal to the base return (Basisertrag), because the advance lump sum is capped at the year's increase in value.

On a sale, the **FIFO principle** applies. Under Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG (Income Tax Act), the units bought first are deemed to be sold first, per securities account and without any choice. In a portfolio built up over twenty years, these are the oldest and cheapest units, that is, those with the highest unrealised gain. Anyone who later wants to withdraw only “a little” thereby triggers the highest possible tax. This can only be influenced by using separate securities accounts; an instruction to the bank is not enough.

mitnehmen: Above all, a savings plan replaces twelve timing decisions a year with an automatic process, and such decisions are what create the investor return gap of 1.2 percentage points a year.
The cost-averaging effect exists arithmetically but is neutral for returns; the average purchase price is always below the average price, even in a market that only falls.

Phasing in an existing sum reduces the fluctuation of the outcome at the expense of expected return; in around two out of three historical twelve-month windows, the immediate lump-sum investment came out ahead.
The durability and growth of the instalment matter more than its size; 3% escalation raises the final value from €301,000 to €420,000, because the savings rate grows automatically.
Fees per execution weigh many times more heavily than the frequency; 1.75% of the instalment costs around €5,300 over 30 years, while switching from monthly to weekly brings at most around €560.

begriffe.text: The average purchase price of a savings plan is the harmonic mean of the purchase prices and is therefore always below their arithmetic mean. The effect follows necessarily from the arithmetic and is neutral for returns. It describes a lower average market exposure and brings no additional return.
Charge per savings plan execution, either as a fixed amount or as a percentage of the instalment. It acts like a permanent cut in every instalment. With an instalment of €300, 1.75% costs €63 a year.
Automatic annual increase in the monthly contribution by a fixed percentage, typically 1% to 10%. It keeps the savings rate constant without a new decision being needed every year.

FIFO stands for “first in, first out”. Under Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG, the units bought first are deemed to be sold first on a sale, per securities account and without any choice for the investor. With long-running savings plans, these are the units with the largest unrealised gain.
